requirements: Every conforming container or bag of Boric Acid must bear the BIS Standard Mark (ISI Mark) along with the manufacturer's licence number (CM/L).

Special Quality (SQ) grade material (intended for use in capacitors, electronics, nuclear energy, foundries, and fire proofing) must be supplied exclusively in the form of granules to prevent caking and ensure handling stability.
Technical and Explosive grade materials can be supplied in the form of granules, powder, crystals, or flakes, and must be free from odour, dirt, visible impurities, and foreign matter.
Boric Acid (as H3BO3) must be a minimum of 99.5 percent by mass for all grades, with moisture content limited to a maximum of 0.2 percent by mass.

For technical grade (TECH) applications, additional polishing compounds must conform to specified ranges: Chloride (as Cl) of 0.05 to 0.15 percent by mass, and Sulphate (as SO4) of 0.15 to 0.25 percent by mass. These are necessary additives that reduce corrosion in end-user industrial environments (such as steel furnaces).
Explosive grade material must satisfy tighter limits for polishing compounds to ensure chemical stability: Chloride (as Cl) must be below 0.05% and Sulphate (as SO4) must be below 0.15%.

Each bag or container must be legibly and indelibly marked with: manufacturer name or trade-mark, product name, grade (Special Quality, Technical, or Explosive), physical form (Granules, Powder, Crystals, or Flakes), batch/lot number, net mass, month and year of manufacture, and shelf-life expiry date.
Sodium impurities must be tested via flame photometry as per IS 9497, using a corrected wavelength of 589 nm (correcting a typo in the original text which specified '589 mm') [1].

The minimum allowed purity of the chemical must be 99.0 percent by mass, tested in accordance with the acidimetric titration method specified in Annex B.
The relative density of the liquid compound at 20/20 °C must be a minimum of 1.001, evaluated per Annex C.
The colour of morpholine must be clear and light, not exceeding 15 units on the Platinum-Cobalt (Pt-Co) scale when tested per IS 3025 (Part 4).
Boiling range characteristics must be highly controlled: the temperature must remain between 125 °C and 129 °C for 90 percent recovery of the distilled fraction when tested per IS 5298.
To prevent particulate fouling, residues on evaporation must not exceed a maximum of 1000 mg/l (Annex D), and the ash content must not exceed 0.003 g/100 ml (Annex E).
Trace contaminants must remain within low safety thresholds: Silica (as SiO2) is restricted to a maximum of 5 ppm, and Chloride (as Cl) is limited to a maximum of 5 ppm.
The maximum permissible concentration for trace iron (Fe), copper (Cu), and nickel (Ni) impurities is strictly limited to 5 ppm each.

In case of determination by ICP-OES or ICP-MS, sample preparation must be followed as per F-1. Reagents include de-ionized water, 96% H2SO4, 70% HClO4, 65% HNO3, 36% HCl, 99.9% Cs2SO4, and a mixed acid (HNO3:H2SO4:HClO4, 2:1:1 ratio) or Acid Mixture 1 (H2SO4:HNO3, 39:1 ratio with 2.2 g/l Cs2SO4). Weigh 0.35 g to 0.40 g of sample into the automated digestion system, add acid mixture, crack at 320 °C, completely digest organic remnants at 160 °C, evaporate to dryness, boil residue with 5% HCl, and perform duplicate determinations to report the mean value.

In case of determination by ICP-OES or ICP-MS, sample preparation must be followed as per F-2. Reagents include 50% HCl, 0.4 g K2CO3-Na2CO3 and 0.1 g Na2B4O7 (soda-borax, 4:1 w/w mix). Pre-condition a platinum dish at 550 °C for 10 min. Weigh 100 g to 115 g sample in portions of 20 g to 40 g into the Pt dish, burn above a Bunsen burner, incinerate residues at 550 °C for 30 min in a muffle furnace, homogenize residue with soda-borax mix, melt over open flame, dissolve cooled melt cake in 6 ml HCl and 10 ml water, heat, and dilute to 50 ml for duplicate determinations.

Prescribes two spectrophotometric methods—thioglycolic acid and o-phenanthroline—designed to measure trace levels of iron in parts-per-million or parts-per-billion ranges.

Ferric iron (Fe3+) is reduced to ferrous iron (Fe2+) using stannous chloride (SnCl2) in a hot hydrochloric acid medium. The excess SnCl2 is neutralized using saturated mercuric chloride (HgCl2), which forms a silky white precipitate of mercurous chloride (Hg2Cl2).

To prevent hydrochloric acid from being oxidized by the titrant, Zimmermann-Reinhardt solution (containing manganous sulphate, phosphoric acid, and sulphuric acid) is added prior to titrating against standard 0.1 N potassium permanganate. Phosphoric acid complexes with yellow Fe3+ ions to form a colorless ferric phosphate complex, ensuring a sharp pink endpoint.

Similar reduction is performed using stannous chloride and mercuric chloride. The Fe2+ ions are subsequently titrated against standard potassium dichromate solution in an acidic medium using diphenylamine or sodium diphenylamine sulphonate indicator to yield a sharp violet-blue endpoint.

Thioglycolic acid reduces trivalent ferric iron (Fe3+) almost instantaneously to divalent ferrous iron (Fe2+), while simultaneously reacting with the Fe2+ ions in an alkaline ammonium hydroxide medium to form a highly stable, intensely colored reddish-purple coordination complex measured spectrophotometrically at 535 nm to 540 nm.

Ferrous iron (Fe2+) reacts with 1,10-phenanthroline to form an orange-red chelate complex, [Fe(o-phen)3]2+, which is measured spectrophotometrically at 510 nm. Any Fe3+ present in the sample must first be quantitatively reduced using thioglycolic acid or hydroxylamine hydrochloride to estimate total iron.

Iron content in ppm (as Fe) is calculated using the formula: Iron (as Fe) ppm = C * 25 / W, where C is the concentration of iron from the standard calibration curve in micrograms per milliliter (ug/mL), and W is the weight in grams (g) of the sample contained in the test aliquot.

certification.description: Strict Statutory Mandatory Certification. Under the 'Footwear made from Leather and other Materials (Quality Control) Order' (QCO) issued by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Government of India, all general-purpose shoes manufactured, imported, distributed, or sold in India must carry the mandatory BIS Standard Mark (ISI Mark). Manufacturing, importing, stocking, or selling uncertified shoes in the domestic market is a criminal offense under the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 2016. Micro and small enterprises (MSEs) are granted specific delayed implementation timelines, and export-only shipments are exempt. Precious metal hallmarking is completely inapplicable to everyday consumer footwear.
requirements: Every pair of general-purpose shoes must be legibly and indelibly marked or labeled on the inner lining, side of the tongue, or collar with the BIS Standard Mark (ISI Mark) accompanied by the manufacturer's registered licence number (CM/L).
Shoes are categorized into Kids (standard English sizes per IS 1638) and Adults (Type 1 and Type 2 sizes per IS 1638) to ensure correct anatomical fit and prevent premature joint wear.

Component raw materials must conform to strict physical-chemical limits: Upper (Cl 6.1.1 and 6.1.2), Lining (Cl 6.2), Insole (Cl 6.3), Insock (Cl 6.4), Outsole (Cl 6.5), Midsole (Cl 6.6), and Toe and Counter Stiffeners (Cl 6.7).

Under Amendment No. 1, the bond strength at joint interfaces must comply with strict limits: a) Adults (Type 1): minimum 2.5 N/mm (or 2.0 N/mm in case of material tear); b) Adults (Type 2): minimum 1.5 N/mm (or 1.0 N/mm in case of material tear); c) Kids: minimum 1.0 N/mm (or 1.0 N/mm in case of material tear) [1].

For Adults (Type 1) general-purpose shoes, water-repellent uppers must pass a rigorous dynamic wetting test on an oscillating platform [1]. The test piece (grain surface in contact with ground, cut parallel to backbone) is continuously wetted on a perforated platform (roughened surface) and flexed/compressed under an 80 ± 5 N force by a 120 mm diameter roller [1]. The machine oscillates at 20 ± 1 cycles/min with an amplitude of 50 ± 2 mm [1]. Absorbent cellulosic boards (1.6 mm thickness, 1 200 g/m² mass) and undyed cotton gauze are used to detect initial water penetration [1]. Requirements mandate: a) Water penetration: No water penetration till 30 minutes; b) Water absorption: maximum 25 percent by weight [1].

For shoes intended for cold regions, uppers must undergo flexing tests at -5°C on a flexing machine [1]. After 25,000 continuous flexes, the upper must show zero crack initiation, fat spue, or structural failure [1].

The finished footwear must satisfy mandatory physical thresholds, including: a) Interlayer bond strength (midsole to outsole): minimum 1.5 N/mm; b) Whole shoe flexing (Ross flexing machine); c) Slip resistance: dynamic coefficient of friction (COF) of minimum 0.3 on wet and dry quarry tiles; d) Attachment strength of straps and buckles/D-rings; e) Attachment strength of strap velcro; f) Strength of eyelet attachment; g) Heel pull-off strength; h) Top piece attachment strength; i) Seam strength (minimum 4.0 N/mm); j) Whole shoe topline strength; k) Outsole abrasion resistance (maximum volume loss).

All shoe components must meet the strict chemical restricted substances limits of IS 17011 to prevent toxic exposure: a) Allergenic & carcinogenic disperse dyes: < 1 mg/l; b) Aromatic amines from Azo dyes: < 20 mg/kg; c) Chromium (VI) in leather: < 3 mg/kg; d) Dimethyl fumarate (DMFu): < 0.1 mg/kg; e) Formaldehyde: Kids < 20 mg/kg; Adults (direct skin contact) < 75 mg/kg; Adults (no direct skin contact) < 100 mg/kg; f) Lead content (as Pb): extremely low limits (typically <= 2 ppm in straps or up to 100 ppm overall).

The manufacturer must maintain a strict Quality Assurance Plan (QAP). Under BIS footwear guidelines, all shoes of the same type and variety produced within 10,000 pairs or a fortnight's production (whichever is earlier) constitute a single 'control unit'. Representative samples must be drawn randomly and tested in rotation to verify continuous lot compliance.

Since IS 18001 is a management system standard rather than a physical consumer product, it does not carry an individual physical 'ISI Mark' standard mark on a consumer label. Instead, organizations apply to accredited third-party registrars (such as the BIS Management Systems Certification Department) to undergo a rigorous multi-stage audit and obtain an official 'OHSMS Certificate of Registration' [1]. This certification enhances public image, minimizes liability risks, and demonstrates strict compliance with India's central and state Factories Acts [2, 3].
requirements: Top management must define, document, and endorse an OH&S policy that is appropriate to the nature and scale of the organization's risks, includes a commitment to continual improvement and legal compliance, is made known to all employees, and is reviewed periodically [4, 5].

Requires identifying, accessing, and tracking central, state, and local legal requirements (and changes thereto) attributable to the organization's activities and hazards, ensuring relevant information is communicated to employees [6, 7].

Top management must designate, document, and communicate OH&S responsibilities, authorities, and reporting lines for all levels—including sub-contractors and visitors. A senior management representative must be assigned to oversee the OHSMS [4, 8].

Requires identifying operations associated with significant risks and executing them under specified conditions. This mandates implementing procedures for personal protective equipment (PPE) control, access segregation, and high-integrity testing of operator protection, physical guarding, and automatic shutdown systems [9-11].

Mandates establishing and periodically testing procedures to identify and respond to emergency situations. For large installations, plans must be prepared in consultation with municipal or state disaster planning teams. Appropriate first-aid facilities must be matched to site hazards, including stabilization protocols for remote sites [12, 13].

A mandatory post-incident recovery plan (CIRP) must be established, covering: clear responsibilities, confidential post-trauma 'defusing' immediately after the event, emotional 'de-briefing' for employees, and counseling for victims' families [14, 15].

Requires establishing and maintaining procedures for the identification, storage, protection, retrieval, retention, and disposal of records to demonstrate system conformity and trace performance outcomes [16].

Requires conducting internal audits of the OH&S management system at planned intervals to verify that the system conforms to planned arrangements, has been properly implemented and maintained, and to identify areas for continual improvement [16].

Establishes a three-dimensional matrix to evaluate risk levels (Trivial, Tolerable, Moderate, Substantial, or Intolerable) based on the probability of occurrence (Highly Unlikely, Unlikely, Likely) and the severity of harm (Slightly Harmful, Harmful, Extremely Harmful) [17].

Requires reviewing any proposed risk control action plan before implementation, checking if revised controls achieve tolerable levels, if new hazards are created, and if the solution is cost-effective and accepted by employees [18].

Heel pins must be exactly 29 mm ± 1 mm long for leather soles and 25 mm ± 1 mm long for rubber heels.

The steel toe cap must withstand a drop-weight impact test where a mass is dropped from a height of exactly 508 mm ± 5 mm onto a vertical plunger, transferring a mandatory impact energy of 14 kgf.m (approx. 137 Joules) onto the toe cap.

requirements: Under this second revision, the method involving visual detection of the end-point is completely deleted due to color change detection difficulties in dark or colored chemical solutions, shifting entirely to direct electrometric titration and electrometric back-titration.
The volumetric determination of water is based on the reaction of water while oxidizing mono-alkyl sulphite to mono-alkyl sulphate using iodine in a 1:1 stoichiometric water-to-iodine ratio.

Incorporates guidelines and reference options for using commercially available, non-pyridine-based Karl Fischer reagents to resolve occupational safety, health, and odor concerns associated with toxic pyridine vapor.

Methanol solvent must be highly anhydrous (max 0.05 percent water by mass). If necessary, it must be dried by distillation from magnesium turnings activated with iodine, and protected from atmospheric moisture using a guard tube filled with anhydrous aluminium sodium silicate or activated silica gel.

For chemical products containing active carbonyl groups (such as aldehydes and ketones), the standard recommends replacing methanol with 2-methoxyethanol (ethylene glycol monomethyl ether) to stabilize titration volumes and prevent acetal/ketal-forming side reactions that generate false water.

Direct titration detects the end point by depolarization of the cathode. While water is present, polarization opposes current. At the exact moment water is completely consumed, the first trace of excess iodine depolarizes the platinum electrodes, causing a sudden, permanent increase in current intensity.
In back-titration, an excess of Karl Fischer reagent is added to the sample and titrated back with standard water-methanol solution until the galvanometer pointer moves suddenly to zero.

The water equivalent (T) of the Karl Fischer reagent (in mg H2O/mL) is calibrated by dividing the mass of liquid water or sodium tartrate dihydrate by the net volume of Karl Fischer reagent consumed, taking into account water-methanol back-titration values.
Sodium tartrate dihydrate is specified as the primary crystalline standard for calibrating water equivalents, applying a precise mathematical factor of 0.1566 to its mass.
All observed or calculated test and analytical values must be mathematically rounded off in accordance with IS 2:1960 to match the significant places of the specified limits.
